### actor.client — Client

The party paying for the seat when the company is not its own customer. Signs the contract the requisition depends on, and often holds a gate the candidate never sees named.

- Decides: Whether the contract that funds the seat is signed, extended or cancelled
- Decides: The rate the seat bills at, which the band is derived from
- Decides: Approval of the profiles submitted against the contract, where the contract gives them that right
- Decides: Their own interview round, after the employer's loop has already said yes
- Decides: How many seats the engagement needs, and by when
- Cannot see: What the employer's own funnel did to reach the profiles they are shown
- Cannot see: What the candidate was told about who is deciding, and when
- Cannot see: The margin between the rate they pay and the salary the candidate is offered
- Cannot see: What declining a profile without a reason costs the person behind it
- Measured on: Fill the seats the engagement needs without carrying employment obligations
- Measured on: Keep the option to end the engagement without ending anyone's employment — that is what the vendor is for
- Measured on: Pay for delivery, not for the search that produced it
- Could do (low): Let your round be named in the process the candidate is told — Where the contract gives the client a profile approval or an interview, the candidate ends up waiting on a party no message has named. Allowing the vendor to state that stage — one client review, expected turnaround — costs no confidentiality and converts an unexplained silence into a stated step. Costs: A named stage invites questions when it overruns; an unnamed one never has to answer for itself.
- Could do (low): State in the brief whether the seat is funded or bid-conditional — A search run against an unsigned bid is a real search for a conditional seat. The vendor's recruiters can only disclose what the brief states, so the one sentence that makes outreach honest — this role opens when the contract signs — has to originate here. Costs: A bid the market can see is a bid competitors can see; some clients treat the existence of the search as confidential.
- Could do (low): Return profile decisions on a stated clock, with a category — The employer cannot tell the candidate what it was never told. A decline that arrives as one of three categories — profile, rate, timing — on a stated turnaround lets the vendor close records with a reason instead of a template, without exposing anything commercially sensitive. Costs: A category is a commitment; 'no' with no category can no longer be sent.

### actor.employer_policy — Employer policy

Finance, leadership and the people function: the layer that authorises headcount, fixes bands and writes the rules the funnel executes. Never meets a candidate.

- Decides: Whether a requisition is funded, and whether it stays funded
- Decides: The band and the levelling grid
- Decides: Whether postings must be published externally regardless of internal candidates
- Decides: What may be disclosed, and what must not be
- Cannot see: What a freeze looks like from the far end of a five-round process
- Cannot see: How a compliance posting reads to someone who spent six weeks on it
- Cannot see: The cumulative candidate hours a policy consumes
- Measured on: Optionality: an approved requisition that can be paused costs less than one that cannot
- Measured on: Consistency and legal defensibility across every hire
- Measured on: Cost control, on a cycle measured in quarters rather than in conversations
- Could do (medium): Publish the band on the posting itself — The band and the levelling grid are set in this layer, and nothing downstream can disclose a number this layer has not released. Publishing it turns the reconciliation at bar.compensation_levelling_reconciliation into arithmetic rather than a conversation that happens for the first time after the panel. Costs: The published number becomes a commitment the band cannot be quietly revised against mid-search, and it is legible to everyone already employed at that level.
- Could do (high): Sign the headcount before the role is published — This layer decides whether a requisition is funded, and bar.headcount_executive_budget_approval is the only gate that stops a process after every person the candidate met has said yes. Moving the finance signature ahead of publication makes the later approval a countersignature, so a published role is one whose headcount already exists. Costs: Budget is committed at publication rather than at the offer, and a requisition funded in advance is harder to pause than one approved at the end.
- Could do (medium): Expire the listing when its authorisation lapses — Whether a requisition stays funded is decided here, and that fact reaches no configuration screen on its own. A rule that withdraws the listing when authorisation lapses, and notifies everyone still inside the process, closes the gap between the decision and what the page shows. Costs: A paused search cannot be kept warm: reopening means another trip through the approval chain and a posting that restarts from zero applicants, which is a direct charge on this layer's optionality.
- Could do (medium): State on the posting that an internal candidacy exists — The rule that a role is published externally regardless of an internal candidate sits in this layer, and so does what the posting may say. One line stating that an internal candidacy is in process gives an external applicant, at the point of applying, the fact the panel already has. Costs: The external pool for those postings shrinks, which weakens the same posting as evidence of an open search, and an internal candidacy goes in writing before the search has concluded.
- Could do (medium): Narrow the checks and show the candidate any discrepancy — Which checks a role requires, and whether a third-party record is put to the candidate before it decides anything, are both settled in this layer. At bar.reference_background_verification a mismatch between a vendor record and an application holds the offer, and only a policy rule makes the candidate's account part of the file before the hold becomes a decision. Costs: Every discrepancy adds a round trip before countersignature, and the single standard check pack has to be split by role instead of running identically on every hire.

### actor.hiring_manager — Hiring manager

The person the role reports to, and the panel they convene. Sets the bar, owns the outcome, and is doing this alongside the work the role exists to absorb.

- Decides: The requirements as written, and the ones only they know about
- Decides: Who interviews and what they ask
- Decides: The level a candidate is assessed at
- Decides: Whether a split panel becomes a hire
- Cannot see: What the same candidate showed in rounds they did not attend
- Cannot see: How the requirements read to someone outside the team
- Cannot see: What the search is costing the people covering the gap
- Measured on: Avoid a bad hire, which is visible and attributed, more than a missed hire, which is neither
- Measured on: Fill the gap without the ramp-up cost of someone who needs teaching
- Measured on: Keep the team's own delivery on track while running the loop
- Could do (medium): Write the requirement list from last quarter's work — The requirements as written belong to this actor, and the list is what the keyword filter and the recruiter's screen are both built from. Checking each line against what the team delivered last quarter separates what the job uses from what a previous strong candidate happened to have. A year count larger than the age of the technology is checkable before the posting goes up. Costs: A shorter list brings more applications into a funnel this actor's own team staffs, and it gives up the requirement page as the argument for a higher level and a wider band.
- Could do (low): Put the house preferences into the interview brief — This actor sets what each interviewer asks, and holds the requirements only they know about. A preference about architecture or about vertical experience that is not in the brief is still scored in the room, and the candidate cannot design against a criterion they were not given. Costs: A preference in writing is open to challenge from the panel and from the recruiter, and one that cannot be put into a sentence does not make it into the brief.
- Could do (medium): Cap the take-home and floor the review time — The exercise and who reviews it are both this actor's to set. Work built over hours and read in minutes is scored on whatever the reader happened to open, and the note that comes out of it describes the review rather than the submission. Capping the candidate's hours without a floor under the reviewer's minutes moves the asymmetry rather than closing it. Costs: A three-hour sample carries less to go on, so more of the decision falls to the panel, and twenty minutes from each of two reviewers comes out of a sprint the team is already behind on.
- Could do (medium): Agree the decision rule before the first conversation — Whether a split panel becomes a hire is this actor's decision, and a unanimity requirement settles it in advance: one dissent and three produce the same outcome. Writing the rule down before the loop starts, including who breaks a tie, keeps an even split from being written up as a finding about the candidate. Costs: Naming the tiebreaker means this actor signs a hire the panel did not agree on, and a hire that goes wrong is visible for a year and carries their name.
- Could do (high): Freeze the requirements once the loop opens — The requirements as written are this actor's; whether a requisition closes is not. Assessments taken against one description do not carry over to another, so a change of stack or scope that arrives mid-loop belongs in the next posting rather than in the scoring of work already done. Everyone already inside is then measured against the description they were given. Costs: The loop runs to the end against a profile the team has moved past, and the change the requirements needed waits for a search that starts again from the posting.
- Could do (medium): Fix the assessed level before the loop opens — The level a candidate is assessed at is this actor's to set, and it is set at the in-depth review whether or not it was written down first. Naming the level, and what evidence meets it, before the loop opens means experience above the band is measured against the requirements rather than against a forecast about how long someone stays. Costs: A level fixed in advance removes the move of recovering a strong candidate at the level below, and where the level was set wrong the search runs again from the posting.

### actor.public_policy_and_industry_standards — Public policy and industry standards

Regulators, labour law, and the conventions the market copies from itself. Sets the outer bounds and moves on a timescale no individual process can wait for.

- Decides: What must be disclosed — pay transparency rules being the clearest current example
- Decides: What automated decision-making is permitted, and what must be explainable
- Decides: Which employment relationships are possible in which jurisdiction
- Cannot see: How a rule is implemented once it reaches a configuration screen
- Cannot see: Practices that are legal, ordinary, and still produce the effects catalogued here
- Measured on: Rules that are enforceable and measurable, which is a narrower set than rules that would help
- Measured on: Not disrupting labour markets faster than they can absorb the change
- Could do (medium): Extend disclosure from the band to the level — A disclosure rule that reaches the band leaves unstated the level the band attaches to, and the level decides where inside the band an offer lands. Requiring the posting to name the level being hired at, and the band for that level, closes the branch of the compensation bind that a band alone leaves open. Costs: A band is a number on a page and a level is a claim about an internal grid, so each complaint needs records the regulator has to ask for separately. It also fixes at publication a level that is currently settled after the panel.
- Could do (medium): Require postings to name where employment is possible — Which employment relationships are possible in which jurisdiction is settled before anyone applies, and it is one of the few facts here that this actor defines rather than regulates at a distance. Requiring the posting to list the jurisdictions the role can actually be contracted in moves that fact to publication day instead of the screening call. Costs: The rule binds a posting readable everywhere to contracts possible in a few places, and the body writing it reaches only its own territory — which one that is, this atlas does not state. The employer must publish an entity map it holds internally, and postings that read as open narrow visibly.
- Could do (medium): Require postings to be dated and withdrawn on closure — What a public posting is — an advertisement, or a statement that funded work exists — is a disclosure question, and that is the question this actor reaches. A rule that a posting carries its publication date and comes down when the search ends makes the difference between an open search and a talent pool observable from outside. Costs: Two dates are cheap to check, but the fact that decides a breach — whether the search had ended — sits in records only the employer holds, so every complaint starts with disclosure. The rule also reaches sourcing that is legal and ordinary, which widens the perimeter it has to defend.
- Could do (high): Require every automated rejection to name its rule — Where an application is ended by a threshold rather than by a reader, whether that decision must be explainable already sits inside this actor's bounds. Attaching the duty to the ending rather than to the message means a rule that closes an application — a missing term, an unmet threshold, an elapsed review window — produces a statement the applicant can check instead of nothing. Costs: The duty is written for an employer and performed by a setting on a configuration screen the rule's author never sees, so the text has to fix responsibility somewhere between the party that buys the system and the party that ships it. Each stated reason is also a statement that can be disputed, and at the volume of ended applications that is a caseload before it is a remedy.
- Could do (medium): Require continuity-based ranking features to be documented and justified — A feature that scores the length of a break sits inside the automated decision-making whose bounds this actor sets, and it is the input that closes the gap-penalty loop. Requiring any ranking input derived from employment continuity to be documented and justified makes its presence checkable, which a prohibition on its own does not. Costs: The rule can only be checked where the feature is named in a model card or a settings screen, so it rests on a documentation duty that lands on a supplier rather than on the employer being regulated. Naming one input leaves its proxies — recency of the last role, density of transitions — outside the text until they are named too.
- Could do (low): Publish a common schema for posting terms and outcomes — The market copies conventions from itself faster than it absorbs rules, and this actor writes conventions as well as rules. A published schema — band, level, stages, jurisdictions, and a decline that names its stage and its criterion — gives the disclosure duties a shape that can be filled in once and read by machine. Costs: A schema carries no obligation, so it is adopted where it is cheaper than what it replaces and nowhere else. The categories fixed in the first version become the ceiling on what is disclosed later, and the body that publishes it owns the revisions for as long as anyone uses it.

### actor.recruiter — Recruiter

The function that moves people through the funnel. Holds the most information about the process and the least authority over its outcome.

- Decides: Which applications are read and in what order
- Decides: What is disclosed at the screen, and when
- Decides: The wording of the rejection
- Decides: Whether a candidate is told a search has stalled
- Cannot see: What the panel actually scored, beyond the recommendation
- Cannot see: Whether finance will approve the headcount this quarter
- Cannot see: What the hiring manager privately requires but has not written down
- Measured on: Move the pipeline; time-to-fill is measured, time-to-clarity is not
- Measured on: Protect the relationship with the hiring manager, who is the internal client
- Measured on: Avoid saying anything that could be quoted back as a commitment
- Could do (medium): State the band before asking for a number — The screen is where compensation first comes up, and the order of the two questions is the recruiter's to set. Saying the band that is on the requisition, before asking what the candidate expects, removes the asymmetry that both branches of the compensation bind run on. Where no band has been set, saying that is also an answer the candidate can act on. Costs: It spends the flexibility of hearing the candidate's figure first, and it puts a number into the conversation that can be quoted back later as a commitment.
- Could do (medium): Name the stage and the criterion that ended it — The wording of the rejection belongs to this seat, and the same message can carry the stage the process ended at, the criterion that was named to the recruiter, and what the process never reached. Where the panel returned a recommendation without a criterion, the message records that no criterion was given, rather than a template sentence standing in its place. What can be written is bounded by what the recruiter was handed. Costs: Each message is written rather than selected, against a clock measured as time-to-fill, and asking the panel for a criterion spends standing with the hiring manager, who is the internal client.
- Could do (medium): Tell everyone still inside when a search stops moving — Whether a candidate learns that a search has stalled is decided in this seat, and it can be decided from what is visible here: the date of the last scheduling activity on the requisition. The message states that date and no more, because whether the headcount returns this quarter is not visible from here. Silence at this point is read as a decision about the candidate. Costs: Candidates who are told make other plans, and the message puts in writing that the internal client's search has stopped, against a seat measured on time-to-fill and on that relationship.
- Could do (medium): Name every stage and its date at the screen — What the process contains, how many conversations it has and when the first decision is due are disclosed at the screen or nowhere, and that disclosure sits in this seat. A candidate holding the list can tell a delay from an ending. When a round is added or a date moves, the same channel carries that within days to everyone already inside. Costs: A stated date is a commitment held against interviewer calendars this seat does not control, so every slip becomes a message that has to be written.
- Could do (medium): Say whether an approved requisition sits behind the call — Outreach and the first conversation are where the recruiter states what the contact is for. Whether a requisition is open and approved, or whether this is a pool for headcount that does not exist yet, is a fact available at the moment of contact. Without it, the silence that follows such a conversation is read as a decision about the candidate. Costs: It costs replies: outreach that states there is no open requisition gives less reason to answer, and reply volume is what the sourcing side of the pipeline is counted in.
- Could do (high): Set the reading order in advance and in writing — Which applications are read and in what order is decided in this seat, and the order can be fixed before the week's queue exists: a stated share of screening capacity for inbound, order of arrival within each source, and no sort on how recently someone was last employed. The rule adds no screening capacity; it decides once where the capacity goes, instead of deciding it profile by profile against the length of the queue. Costs: Reading without that sort covers fewer profiles per hour, and outbound candidates the hiring manager has asked about wait behind inbound ones.

## Processes

### proc.an_application_inside_the_ats — An application inside the ATS

The machine the candidate never sees: what happens to a submitted application between the form and a human being, and the four ways it can end without anyone reading it.

- Subject: one application record · Evidence: unknown
- State submitted (initial, owner actor.candidate): A form submission has been accepted. Fields are validated against the requisition schema; nothing has been interpreted.
- State parsing (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): The document is converted to structured fields. Multi-column layouts, graphics and custom fonts routinely lose whole sections silently.
- State scoring (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): Knockout rules, keyword coverage, years thresholds and ranking features run in sequence, short-circuiting on the first failure.
- State queued (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): The record is above the threshold and waiting. Queue position depends on source: outbound lists are usually read first.
- State reviewed (active, owner actor.recruiter): A recruiter opens the profile. The median attention available per profile is measured in seconds when the queue is deep.
- State advanced (terminal, owner actor.recruiter): The record leaves this machine and enters proc.the_hiring_funnel_end_to_end at the recruiter screen.
- State auto-rejected (terminal, owner actor.ats_vendor): A rule failed. The notification is often queued and sent minutes later, which is what produces a rejection at midnight.
- State human-rejected (terminal, owner actor.recruiter): Someone read it and did not take it forward. What the message says about why is a separate decision, usually a template.
- State expired (terminal, owner actor.ats_vendor): A scheduled job closed the record after a threshold. Nobody read it, and the email it sends is indistinguishable from one that followed a review.
- Transition submitted → parsing (actor.ats_vendor): document accepted · guard: Required fields validate and the file is a supported type.
- Transition parsing → scoring (actor.ats_vendor): fields extracted · guard: Extraction completes, whether or not it recovered the work history.
- Transition scoring → queued (actor.ats_vendor): all rules pass · guard: Every knockout rule passes and the rank clears the advance threshold.
- Transition scoring → auto-rejected (actor.ats_vendor): a rule fails · guard: Any knockout rule fails, or the ranking falls below the threshold.
- Transition queued → reviewed (actor.recruiter): a recruiter opens it · guard: Capacity reaches this position in the queue before the expiry threshold.
- Transition queued → expired (actor.ats_vendor): threshold reached first · guard: The record ages past the configured limit with no review recorded.
- Transition reviewed → advanced (actor.recruiter): short-listed · guard: The profile is put on the active list for outreach.
- Transition reviewed → human-rejected (actor.recruiter): passed over · guard: The recruiter decides not to advance it.

### proc.client_account_hiring_funnel — Client account hiring funnel

From client demand and commercial contract to profile submission, client interview, and placement or unannounced closure.

- Subject: a seat funded by a client contract and the candidate moving towards it · Evidence: unknown
- State demand (initial, owner actor.client): The end client identifies project headcount demand or issues a vendor tender. Budget exists if the contract is signed or is contingent on winning the bid.
- State search-open (active, owner actor.recruiter): Vendor recruiting opens direct outreach or listings. Whether an executed contract or an unawarded bid sits behind it is not disclosed.
- State vendor-screen (active, owner actor.recruiter): Introductory conversation assessing experience and target compensation against the vendor target margin.
- State vendor-technical (active, owner actor.hiring_manager): Technical interview or test task scored against the vendor assessment of the client technical threshold.
- State submitted (active, owner actor.client): The candidate CV is submitted to the client account team for profile review and interview selection.
- State client-interview (active, owner actor.client): Interview conducted directly by client engineering or project management leadership.
- State offer (active, owner actor.recruiter): Compensation package calculated from client billing rate minus required gross margin.
- State verification (active, owner actor.employer_policy): Client-mandated background checks, certifications, and compliance paperwork.
- State placed (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): Contract executed and candidate onboarded onto active client delivery.
- State vendor-declined (terminal, owner actor.recruiter): The search terminates at vendor screening or technical evaluation before client submission.
- State declined-by-client (terminal, owner actor.client): The client declines the CV submission or rejects the candidate after the client interview.
- State closed-unfunded (terminal, owner actor.client): The search closes because the client tender was lost, project budget was cancelled, or the commercial contract was paused.
- State bench-filled (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): The position is allocated to an existing internal specialist released from another account, closing the external process.
- Transition demand → search-open (actor.client): Contract signed or tender profiles required · guard: Commercial contract signed or tender requires candidate CVs
- Transition search-open → vendor-screen (actor.recruiter): Candidate responds to vendor outreach · guard: Outreach accepted and screen booked
- Transition search-open → closed-unfunded (actor.client): Tender lost or client contract cancelled early · guard: Commercial opportunity discontinued before screening
- Transition vendor-screen → vendor-technical (actor.recruiter): Vendor recruiter screen passed · guard: Expectations aligned with client billing margin
- Transition vendor-screen → vendor-declined (actor.recruiter): Screening mismatch or rate misalignment · guard: Candidate rate exceeds allowable vendor margin or skills misfit
- Transition vendor-technical → submitted (actor.hiring_manager): Vendor assessment passed · guard: Technical bar meets vendor expectation of client threshold
- Transition vendor-technical → vendor-declined (actor.hiring_manager): Vendor assessment not met · guard: Profile does not meet vendor internal quality bar
- Transition submitted → client-interview (actor.client): Client approves CV submission · guard: Client manager accepts profile and requests interview
- Transition submitted → declined-by-client (actor.client): Client rejects CV submission · guard: Client manager rejects profile on CV review
- Transition submitted → bench-filled (actor.employer_policy): Vendor assigns internal bench specialist · guard: Bench consultant becomes available mid-search
- Transition submitted → closed-unfunded (actor.client): Client cancels requisition or loses project funding · guard: Client withdraws demand during profile review
- Transition client-interview → offer (actor.client): Client approves interview · guard: Client confirms candidate meets project requirements
- Transition client-interview → declined-by-client (actor.client): Client declines after interview · guard: Client decides against candidate after meeting
- Transition offer → verification (actor.recruiter): Offer agreed and contract drafted · guard: Candidate accepts offer parameters
- Transition offer → closed-unfunded (actor.client): Client pulls project before signing · guard: Client cancels funding after offer extended
- Transition verification → placed (actor.employer_policy): Background check passed and start date confirmed · guard: Verification complete and project onboarding commences

### proc.the_hiring_funnel_end_to_end — The hiring funnel, end to end

From the moment headcount is authorised to a signed contract or a closed search, with the actor who owns each step and what the candidate can see from where they stand.

- Subject: a requisition and the candidate moving through it · Evidence: unknown
- State drafted (initial, owner actor.hiring_manager): A manager writes the role. Level, band and requirements are decided here, usually by copying the last search for the same team.
- State authorised (active, owner actor.employer_policy): Finance and leadership commit budget against the requisition. Approval can lapse or be withdrawn later without the funnel noticing.
- State published (active, owner actor.recruiter): The role is public. It may also be refreshed automatically every thirty days, which looks identical to a new opening.
- State received (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): A record exists and is linked to the requisition. Nothing has been read.
- State machine-screened (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): Parser extraction, keyword thresholds, knockout rules and ranking. Decided in under a second.
- State recruiter-queue (active, owner actor.recruiter): Waiting to be read by a person, in an inbound queue that usually holds more profiles than the week has hours.
- State recruiter-screen (active, owner actor.recruiter): A conversation about compensation, timeline, location and a two-minute version of the last project.
- State technical (active, owner actor.hiring_manager): A live exercise, a take-home, or both, scored against a rubric the candidate does not see.
- State panel (active, owner actor.hiring_manager): Depth, ownership and collaboration, assessed across several interviewers who may be measuring different things.
- State levelling (active, owner actor.employer_policy): The level the panel assigned meets the band finance approved. First time the two are compared.
- State approval (active, owner actor.employer_policy): Manager, director, finance and the talent committee sign off in sequence. Everyone the candidate met has already said yes.
- State offer (active, owner actor.recruiter): A written offer exists. The requisition is still open until the countersignature lands.
- State verification (active, owner actor.employer_policy): A third-party record is compared against what the candidate claimed.
- State hired (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): Contract executed both ways, start date set, onboarding triggered.
- State rejected (terminal, owner actor.recruiter): A decision was made and communicated. What it says about the cause is a separate question entirely.
- State frozen (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): Budget withdrawn or the requisition put on hold. Can happen at any point, including after an offer.
- State lapsed (terminal, owner actor.ats_vendor): No one decided anything. The record aged past a threshold, or the posting was never taken down.
- Transition drafted → authorised (actor.employer_policy): budget signed off · guard: Finance commits headcount against the requisition.
- Transition authorised → published (actor.recruiter): posting goes live · guard: An approved requisition with a written description is published.
- Transition published → received (actor.candidate): application submitted · guard: The candidate applies, or answers outbound outreach.
- Transition received → machine-screened (actor.ats_vendor): rules evaluated · guard: The record is complete enough for the configured rules to run.
- Transition machine-screened → recruiter-queue (actor.ats_vendor): thresholds cleared · guard: Extraction score and every knockout rule pass.
- Transition machine-screened → rejected (actor.ats_vendor): filtered out · guard: Any knockout rule fails, or the ranking falls below the advance threshold.
- Transition recruiter-queue → recruiter-screen (actor.recruiter): short-listed · guard: A person reads the profile and puts it on the list.
- Transition recruiter-queue → lapsed (actor.ats_vendor): aged out · guard: No review happened before the expiry threshold.
- Transition recruiter-screen → technical (actor.recruiter): parameters align · guard: Expectations, timeline and location are compatible, and the profile is submitted to the team.
- Transition recruiter-screen → rejected (actor.recruiter): parameters do not align · guard: Compensation, level, location or availability rules the candidate out before any engineering is discussed.
- Transition technical → panel (actor.hiring_manager): assessment passed · guard: The score clears the rubric threshold.
- Transition technical → rejected (actor.hiring_manager): assessment not passed · guard: The score falls short, or the review is too shallow to find what is there.
- Transition panel → levelling (actor.hiring_manager): panel recommends hire · guard: Consensus reaches the hire threshold.
- Transition panel → rejected (actor.hiring_manager): panel does not reach consensus · guard: A split panel under a unanimity rule defaults to no hire.
- Transition levelling → approval (actor.employer_policy): level and band reconcile · guard: The assigned level and the approved band overlap.
- Transition levelling → rejected (actor.employer_policy): level and band do not reconcile · guard: Expectation sits outside the band and neither the level nor the number moves.
- Transition approval → offer (actor.employer_policy): sign-off complete · guard: Every approver in the chain has cleared it.
- Transition approval → frozen (actor.employer_policy): headcount withdrawn · guard: Budget is pulled or a freeze is announced before the offer is issued.
- Transition offer → verification (actor.candidate): offer accepted · guard: The candidate signs and the checks begin.
- Transition offer → frozen (actor.employer_policy): offer retracted · guard: A freeze reaches an outstanding offer before the countersignature.
- Transition verification → hired (actor.employer_policy): checks clear · guard: No unresolved discrepancy in the third-party record.
- Transition verification → rejected (actor.employer_policy): discrepancy unresolved · guard: A record mismatch or an eligibility bar is not reconciled.
- Transition published → lapsed (actor.ats_vendor): posting outlives the search · guard: Hiring stops but the listing is never withdrawn.
- Transition rejected → published (actor.recruiter): requisition reopened · guard: The search restarts, sometimes with a revised profile, sometimes as an automatic refresh.

### proc.the_path_as_it_is_supposed_to_run — The path as it is supposed to run

One opening, from a real need to a decision the candidate can act on, with each step written as the commitment it is supposed to keep. Every barrier in the registry is a place where one of these commitments stops being kept.

- Subject: one opening, and one candidate moving through it · Evidence: unknown
- State real-need (initial, owner actor.hiring_manager): The requisition describes work that exists now, at a level the team actually needs, inside a band the budget already covers. Nothing here is aspirational: the list of requirements is what the job uses, not what the last four candidates happened to have.
- State published (active, owner actor.recruiter): The posting states the compensation band, the location rules, the stages the process has and roughly how long each takes. It comes down when the search ends.
- State applied (active, owner actor.candidate): The application is submitted and acknowledged. The record holds what the candidate actually wrote, and the candidate can tell that it arrived.
- State machine-check (active, owner actor.ats_vendor): Automation deduplicates, extracts and orders. It does not decide. Where a rule does end an application, the rule is stated and it is one a person would defend out loud.
- State human-read (active, owner actor.recruiter): Every application that clears the mechanical stage is read by someone, and read before the window the posting promised runs out.
- State terms-check (active, owner actor.recruiter): Band, level, location, notice period and start date are put side by side in the first conversation, before any assessment is scheduled. Either side can stop here at no cost to the other.
- State work-sample (active, owner actor.hiring_manager): One timeboxed exercise that resembles the job. The candidate is given the criteria before starting, the timebox is enforced against the evaluator as well, and the same rubric scores everyone.
- State panel (active, owner actor.hiring_manager): Every interviewer knows what they are measuring and that nobody else is measuring it. The rule that turns their scores into a decision is agreed before the first conversation, and no round is added after the process has started.
- State level-and-band (active, owner actor.employer_policy): The level follows from the evidence the panel gathered, and the band was public from the first day. Reconciling them is arithmetic, not a negotiation about whether the band exists.
- State approval (active, owner actor.employer_policy): Headcount was signed before the role was published, so this step is a countersignature rather than a second decision. If the budget goes, the search closes and everyone inside it is told.
- State offer (active, owner actor.recruiter): Salary, level, title, location terms, start date and anything conditional, in writing, with a decision window the candidate agreed to. Nothing in it changes after acceptance.
- State verification (active, owner actor.employer_policy): Only the checks the role actually requires. Where a third-party record disagrees with what the candidate said, the discrepancy is put to the candidate before it decides anything.
- State hired (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): Contract executed both ways on the terms that were on the page from the beginning, with a start date both sides chose.
- State declined (terminal, owner actor.recruiter): Not every candidate is hired, and a decline is not a deviation. What makes it part of this path is that it arrives, it names the stage it happened at and the criterion that decided it, and it says whether applying again is worth anything.
- State closed (terminal, owner actor.employer_policy): A search can legitimately stop: the need changes, the budget goes, someone internal turns out to be right for it. What this path requires is that the posting comes down and every candidate still inside the process is told within days.
- Transition real-need → published (actor.recruiter): posted with its terms · guard: An approved requisition, a band and a described process go live together.
- Transition published → applied (actor.candidate): application submitted · guard: The candidate applies against terms they could read beforehand.
- Transition applied → machine-check (actor.ats_vendor): record processed · guard: The submission is parsed and acknowledged.
- Transition machine-check → human-read (actor.ats_vendor): passed to a person · guard: No automated rule ended it, so a person now has it.
- Transition human-read → terms-check (actor.recruiter): worth a conversation · guard: A person read the profile and wants to talk.
- Transition terms-check → work-sample (actor.recruiter): terms are compatible · guard: Band, level, location and timing work for both sides, said out loud.
- Transition work-sample → panel (actor.hiring_manager): work meets the rubric · guard: The exercise was scored against the criteria the candidate was given.
- Transition panel → level-and-band (actor.hiring_manager): panel decides by its rule · guard: The agreed decision rule returns a hire.
- Transition level-and-band → approval (actor.employer_policy): level lands inside the band · guard: The evidence-assigned level maps to a point in the published band.
- Transition approval → offer (actor.employer_policy): countersigned · guard: The approval that existed before publication is confirmed.
- Transition offer → verification (actor.candidate): offer accepted · guard: The candidate accepts a complete written offer inside the agreed window.
- Transition verification → hired (actor.employer_policy): checks clear · guard: Nothing proportionate to the role is unresolved.
- Transition human-read → declined (actor.recruiter): declined after reading · guard: A person decided no, and said at which stage and on what criterion.
- Transition terms-check → declined (actor.recruiter): terms are incompatible · guard: The gap is named in the same conversation, before any assessment is booked.
- Transition work-sample → declined (actor.hiring_manager): work did not meet the rubric · guard: The score is below the shared criteria, and the criterion is named.
- Transition panel → declined (actor.hiring_manager): decision rule returns no hire · guard: The rule agreed beforehand returns no hire, and which dimension decided it is stated.
- Transition level-and-band → declined (actor.employer_policy): level and expectation do not meet · guard: The published band and the candidate's stated expectation do not overlap, which both sides already knew.
- Transition verification → declined (actor.employer_policy): discrepancy stands · guard: The candidate was shown the discrepancy and it remains unresolved.
- Transition published → closed (actor.employer_policy): need changed · guard: The work no longer exists, and the posting comes down the same week.
- Transition approval → closed (actor.employer_policy): budget withdrawn · guard: Headcount is pulled, and every candidate in the process is told within days.
- Transition offer → closed (actor.employer_policy): offer withdrawn and explained · guard: An outstanding offer cannot stand, and the candidate is told why, in writing, immediately.

## Eras

### era.zero_rates_and_a_same_year_deduction — Zero rates and a same-year deduction

For over a decade money cost nothing to borrow and engineering payroll reduced taxable income in the year it was paid. Both facts were policy, both were durable, and together they made an empty seat more expensive than a wrong hire.

- Span: 2008–2019
- The money: From 16 December 2008 the US policy rate sat at its floor for seven years, and the euro-area deposit rate was cut to zero in July 2012 and below zero in June 2014. Under section 174 as it then stood, research and experimental expenditures could be deducted in the year they were paid rather than charged to capital account. Borrowing to fund growth was close to free, and payroll spent building product reduced taxable income immediately.
- What it did to hiring: Headcount was the standard use of raised capital. A salary was a current-year deduction and the return on a hire was measured in growth rather than in margin, so teams were sized to a funded plan and the plan came before the revenue. A listing route stayed open to companies without trailing profits throughout the period, which meant payroll could run ahead of earnings without closing off the exit.
- How you got in: Demand for people who could do the work ran ahead of supply, so employers hired for potential and trained afterwards. A beginner's salary carried the same immediate deduction as a senior's, which made junior seats cheap to fund against the cost of leaving a seat empty. Self-teaching, a short conversion course and a first job with training attached were ordinary routes in.
- What closed it: Not by a contraction. In March 2020 the same policy floor was reimposed and fund flows stepped up by a multiple, and hiring plans were sized to capital raised rather than to current revenue.
- 0.00–0.25% — US federal funds target range, held at its floor (16 Dec 2008 – 15 Dec 2015, evidence.federal_funds_target_range_and_effective_rate_fred)
- 0.00% → −0.50% — ECB deposit facility rate, at or below zero (11 Jul 2012 – 26 Jul 2022, evidence.ecb_deposit_facility_rate_fred)
- 100% — Research and development payroll deductible in the year it was paid (to tax year 2021, evidence.26_u_s_c_174_as_it_stood_before_2022)
- 15–43% a year — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2011–2021, evidence.technology_ipo_profitability_1980_2025_ritter)

### era.the_record_funding_years — The record funding years

Two years in which the policy floor returned and venture funding roughly doubled its previous record. Headcount plans were set against committed capital rather than against bookings, and the terms of entry were set on the candidate's side.

- Span: 2020–2021
- The money: The policy rate returned to 0.00–0.25% on 16 March 2020 and stayed there for two years. US venture-backed companies raised $329.6 billion in 2021 against a previous record of $166.6 billion in 2020, and global venture investment reached $671 billion. The listing window stayed open to companies without earnings: of 121 US technology listings in 2021, 21% were profitable on trailing twelve-month earnings.
- What it did to hiring: With several years of funding raised at once, headcount was planned against committed capital rather than against bookings, and roles were opened before the work that would fill them was specified. Time-to-fill became the operative constraint, so loops were shortened, offers raised and candidate pools widened across locations. Recruiting functions were themselves staffed to the expanded plan.
- How you got in: Employers competed for candidates, so entry terms were set on the candidate's side: compressed interview loops, offers made on shorter evidence, and pay set by competing bids. Entry-level and career-change intake ran at volume, because the alternative was leaving funded seats empty. Holding a current job was not a precondition, and changing employer was the ordinary way to raise pay.
- What closed it: Two dated changes. The target range left the floor on 17 March 2022, and for tax years beginning after 31 December 2021 any amount paid in connection with developing software had to be capitalised and amortised over five years — so a developer's salary stopped reducing taxable income in the year it was paid.
- $329.6B — US venture-backed companies raised (2021, against $166.6B in 2020, evidence.pitchbook_nvca_venture_monitor_q4_2021)
- $671B — Global venture capital invested (2021, evidence.kpmg_venture_pulse_q4_2021)
- 0.00–0.25% — US policy rate, back at its floor (16 Mar 2020 – 16 Mar 2022, evidence.federal_funds_target_range_and_effective_rate_fred)
- 21% of 121 — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2021, evidence.technology_ipo_profitability_1980_2025_ritter)

### era.rates_up_payroll_repriced — Rates up, payroll repriced

The policy rate reached its cycle peak, technology equities repriced, every stage of the private funding chain contracted at once, and software payroll became something to amortise rather than deduct. The correction ran through announced reductions rather than through attrition.

- Span: 2022–2023
- The money: The federal funds target range reached a cycle peak of 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023 and was held there for about fourteen months, and the technology-weighted NASDAQ Composite fell 36.4% from its November 2021 close to its December 2022 low. Every stage of the private chain contracted together: US venture deal value fell from $348.0 billion in 2021 to $170.6 billion in 2023, exit value hit a decade low of $61.5 billion, and new fund commitments fell to a six-year low of $66.9 billion. From tax years beginning after 31 December 2021, software development costs were amortised over five years for domestic research and fifteen for foreign research instead of being deducted when paid.
- What it did to hiring: Payroll was now both harder to refinance and slower to deduct, so plans were cut to the capital already in hand. Reductions were announced rather than absorbed through attrition: a tracker of publicly reported technology layoffs records 165,269 employees in 2022 and 265,660 in 2023, its highest year. Open requisitions were closed and filled positions eliminated, and the recruiting capacity built for the previous era was itself reduced.
- How you got in: Hiring narrowed to the replacement of specific departures, which meant a posted role described work someone had recently been doing. The evidence employers would accept narrowed with it: recent experience in the same title, at similar scale, in the same stack. The routes that worked when employers hired for potential produced no offers, because the seats being filled were defined by an incumbent's job description rather than by a plan.
- What closed it: The financial conditions reversed without the reduction reversing. The target range came off its peak on 18 September 2024 and the immediate domestic deduction was restored by statute in July 2025, but the headcount removed during the correction was not restored — so the reduced level carried forward as the baseline rather than as a trough.
- 5.25–5.50% — Peak US federal funds target range (27 Jul 2023 – 18 Sep 2024, evidence.fomc_policy_rate_decisions_open_market_operations)
- −36.4% — NASDAQ Composite, record close to cycle low (19 Nov 2021 – 28 Dec 2022, evidence.nasdaq_composite_index_fred)
- $348.0B → $170.6B — US venture deal value (2021 → 2023, evidence.pitchbook_nvca_venture_monitor_q4_2023)
- $61.5B — US venture exit value, a decade low (2023, evidence.pitchbook_nvca_venture_monitor_q4_2023)
- 5 years domestic, 15 foreign — Software payroll amortised rather than deducted (tax years from 2022, evidence.26_u_s_c_174_after_the_2017_amendment)
- 165,269 → 265,660 — Tracked technology layoffs, not a census (2022 → 2023, evidence.tracked_technology_layoffs_layoffs_fyi)

### era.a_fixed_number_of_seats — A fixed number of seats

The conditions that made hiring expensive were reversed; the number of positions was not. The contraction now runs through the hiring channel rather than the separation channel, which is why it is competition for a fixed and shrinking number of seats rather than a shortage of qualified people.

- Span: 2024–2026
- The money: The tax treatment that penalised payroll was undone: section 174A, added on 4 July 2025, allows domestic research expenditure to be deducted when paid for tax years beginning after 31 December 2024, balances capitalised under the 2022–2024 rules may be recovered in one year or over two, and smaller taxpayers may elect back to 2022. Policy rates came off their cycle peak in September 2024. The inputs that made hiring expensive were reversed. The number of positions was not.
- What it did to hiring: The contraction runs through the hiring channel, not the separation channel. Official gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025 — down 28.9% — while official layoffs and discharges in the same series were roughly flat at 451,000, 399,000, 395,000 and 447,000. Openings averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026. Sector payrolls fell from 3,115,000 in November 2022 to 2,780,000 in July 2026.
- How you got in: Incumbents vacate few seats: the information-sector quits rate was 1.1% in June 2026 against 1.9% in June 2022, and the total-private hires rate 3.7% against 4.7%. Applications per open role rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025 across one platform's benchmark. Software postings ran 69.3% senior and 4.5% entry-level in the first quarter of 2026, and payroll records show employment of developers aged 22–25 down close to 20% from its late-2022 peak while employment at older ages in the same occupation did not fall. Entry now means succeeding a specific incumbent rather than being trained into a funded seat.
- 100% — Immediate deduction restored for domestic research (tax years from 2025, evidence.26_u_s_c_174a_domestic_research_expenditures)
- 1,270,000 → 903,000 — Gross hires, US information sector (2022 → 2025, evidence.hires_information_sector_bls_jolts)
- 451,000 → 447,000 — Layoffs and discharges, US information sector — roughly flat (2022 → 2025, evidence.layoffs_and_discharges_information_sector_bls_jolts)
- 224,000/mo → 90,000 — Job openings, US information sector (2022 average → Jun 2026, evidence.job_openings_information_sector_bls_jolts)
- 3,115,000 → 2,780,000 — Information-sector payrolls (Nov 2022 → Jul 2026, evidence.us_information_sector_employment_bls_ces)
- 1.9% → 1.1% — Quits rate, US information sector (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, evidence.quits_rate_information_sector_bls_jolts)
- 4.7% → 3.7% — Hires rate, total private (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, evidence.hires_rate_total_private_bls_jolts)
- 116 → 244 — Applications received per open role, one platform's benchmark (2022 → 2025, evidence.applications_per_opening_greenhouse_hiring_benchmarks)
- 69.3% senior, 4.5% entry — Software postings by level, one job board (Q1 2026, evidence.seniority_mix_of_software_postings_indeed_hiring_lab)
- ≈ −20% — Employment of software developers aged 22–25 (late 2022 → Sep 2025, evidence.employment_of_young_software_developers_stanford_digital_economy_lab)
- 149,023 — Announced technology job cuts, not a census (Jan–Jul 2026, evidence.announced_job_cuts_technology_sector_challenger_gray_christmas)

## Financial records

### record.annual_engineering_department_budget — Annual Engineering Department Budget

Annual operating budget allocation assigned to engineering department headcount.

- Class: budget-line · Owner: inside (actor.employer_policy) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.approved_requisition_funding: requisition headcount allocation · 100% · fraction 1

### record.approved_requisition_funding — Approved Requisition Funding

Headcount allocation and salary band approved for the active requisition.

- Class: requisition-funding · Owner: inside (actor.hiring_manager) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.direct_engineering_payroll: hired candidate compensation · 100% · fraction 1

### record.candidate_liquid_savings — Candidate Liquid Savings

Total liquid personal savings allocated to sustain the job search interval.

- Class: runway · Owner: inside (actor.candidate) · Visibility: observable
- Flow to record.candidate_search_runway: search runway allocation · 100% · fraction 1

### record.candidate_search_runway — Candidate Search Runway

Available runway in months derived from personal savings and monthly burn rate.

- Class: runway · Owner: inside (actor.candidate) · Visibility: observable
- Flow to record.search_month_burn_allocation: monthly living expenditure · 100% · fraction 1

### record.client_project_budget — Client Project Budget

Client total budget line earmarked for third-party engineering services.

- Class: budget-line · Owner: outside-party (actor.client) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.client_services_agreement: master services contract · 100% · fraction 1

### record.client_services_agreement — Client Services Agreement

Commercial contract defining billing rate and seat scope.

- Class: contract · Owner: outside-party (actor.client) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.vendor_margin_and_headcount_allocation: vendor margin split · 100% · fraction 1

### record.contingency_placement_fee_commitment — Contingency Placement Fee Commitment

Placement commission contingent upon candidate starting and passing warranty period.

- Class: placement-fee · Owner: inside (actor.recruiter) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.external_agency_settlement: agency invoice disbursement · 20% · fraction 0.2

### record.direct_engineering_payroll — Direct Engineering Payroll

Direct recurring payroll compensation paid to the employed engineer.

- Class: payroll · Owner: inside (actor.employer_policy) · Visibility: observable

### record.employer_hiring_and_sourcing_budget — Employer Hiring and Sourcing Budget

Operational recruiting budget covering external agency fees and search costs.

- Class: budget-line · Owner: inside (actor.employer_policy) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.contingency_placement_fee_commitment: success fee commitment · 100% · fraction 1

### record.external_agency_settlement — External Agency Settlement

Commercial fee settlement received by the external recruitment agency.

- Class: contract · Owner: outside-party (actor.client) · Visibility: opaque

### record.search_month_burn_allocation — Search-Month Burn Allocation

Living and tooling expenses incurred per month of active job search.

- Class: payroll · Owner: inside (actor.candidate) · Visibility: observable

### record.subcontractor_compensation — Subcontractor Compensation

Net compensation disbursed to the engineer delivering client services.

- Class: payroll · Owner: inside (actor.employer_policy) · Visibility: observable

### record.vendor_margin_and_headcount_allocation — Vendor Margin and Headcount Allocation

Internal vendor allocation splitting client billing into gross margin and candidate cost.

- Class: requisition-funding · Owner: inside (actor.employer_policy) · Visibility: opaque
- Flow to record.subcontractor_compensation: contractor payroll allocation · 75% · fraction 0.75

## Evidence

### evidence.26_u_s_c_174_after_the_2017_amendment — 26 U.S.C. §174 after the 2017 amendment

Section 13206(a) of Public Law 115-97 rewrote section 174 to deny any current deduction for specified research or experimental expenditures and to require them to be charged to capital account and amortised ratably over five years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they are paid or incurred, effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2021. Subsection (c)(3) treats any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of software as such an expenditure, so roughly 10% of a developer's salary was deductible in the year it was paid.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2023 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office. Amendment: Pub. L. 115-97 §13206(a).
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title26/html/USCODE-2023-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### evidence.26_u_s_c_174_as_it_stood_before_2022 — 26 U.S.C. §174 as it stood before 2022

Under section 174(a)(1) as it stood before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act took effect, a taxpayer could treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in connection with a trade or business as expenses not chargeable to capital account, deductible in the year paid or incurred. Payroll spent on building product reduced taxable income in the same year it was spent.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2017 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office.
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2017-title26/html/USCODE-2017-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### evidence.26_u_s_c_174a_domestic_research_expenditures — 26 U.S.C. §174A — domestic research expenditures

Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21, enacted 4 July 2025, added section 174A, which allows a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year notwithstanding section 263, with an election to capitalise and amortise them over not less than 60 months instead. Effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2024.

- 26 U.S.C. §174A, Domestic research or experimental expenditures. Added by Pub. L. 119-21 §70302(a), 4 July 2025.
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/174A

### evidence.a_rejection_issued_without_human_involvement_is_regulated_in_the_eu_gdpr_art_22 — A rejection issued without human involvement is regulated in the EU (GDPR Art. 22)

Under EU data protection law a person has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. Recital 71 names the case directly: "automatic refusal of an online credit application or e-recruiting practices without any human intervention", and states the person should have "the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view, to obtain an explanation of the decision reached after such assessment and to challenge the decision". The distinction the regulation turns on is whether a human was involved at all — the same line the US applicant rules draw, reached from the opposite direction: one governs who must be counted, this one governs what the person may demand. It binds processing in the EU, it says nothing about decisions a human did make, and a rejection preceded by genuine human review falls outside it.

- Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 22 and Recital 71.
- https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/

### evidence.accepted_unconditional_job_offer_is_legally_binding_uk_government_guidance — Accepted unconditional job offers and withdrawal (UK government guidance)

UK government guidance states that an accepted unconditional job offer forms a legally binding employment contract. If an employer then withdraws the offer, the applicant may be able to pursue breach of contract; a conditional offer may be withdrawn when its conditions are not met. The guidance establishes legal consequences, not how often withdrawal occurs or what motive caused it.

- GOV.UK, Job offers: your rights — withdrawing a job offer.
- https://www.gov.uk/job-offers-your-rights

### evidence.algorithmic_bias_in_recruitment_evaluating_resume_screeners_video_analysis_yadav_ahirwar_2026 — Algorithmic Bias In Recruitment: Evaluating Resume Screeners & Video Analysis (Yadav & Ahirwar, 2026)

Reports that unaudited AI resume/video screeners produce a Disparate Impact Ratio below 0.72 for protected groups (improving to 0.88 once mitigation is applied), and documents proxy discrimination through indirect semantic associations with zip code, university tier, and employment-gap language. Caveat: published in the International Journal for Novel Research in Economics, Finance and Management, a venue not indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, or Google Scholar at the time this record was added — treat the underlying methodology as unverified even though the document itself states these figures verbatim.

- Yadav, K., & Ahirwar, K. (2026). Algorithmic Bias In Recruitment: Evaluating the Fairness and Diversity Impact of AI-Driven Resume Screeners and Video Interview Analysis. International Journal for Novel Research in Economics, Finance and Management.
- https://ijnrefm.com/algorithmic-bias-in-recruitment-evaluating-the-fairness-and-diversity-impact-of-ai-driven-resume-screeners-and-video-interview-analysis/

### evidence.announced_job_cuts_technology_sector_challenger_gray_christmas — Announced job cuts, technology sector (Challenger, Gray & Christmas)

A count of announcements of planned job cuts by US-based employers rather than of completed separations; not an official statistic. It reports 133,988 technology-sector cuts announced in 2024, 154,445 in 2025 and 149,023 between January and July 2026 — 67% above the 89,251 announced in the same months of 2025.

- Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Job Cut Announcement Report, July 2026.
- https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Challenger-Report-July-2026.pdf

### evidence.applications_per_opening_greenhouse_hiring_benchmarks — Applications per opening (Greenhouse hiring benchmarks)

Applications received per open role across the reporting platform's customer base rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025, an increase of 111%. The stated dataset covers over 6,000 companies and over 640 million applications, so it measures one platform's customers rather than the labour market.

- Greenhouse, The Hire Standard: hiring benchmarks report, North America, March 2026.
- https://www.greenhouse.com/recruiting-benchmarks

### evidence.applications_per_opening_on_a_national_it_job_board_dou — Applications per opening on a national IT job board (DOU)

Platform-reported counts for a single national IT job board. In March 2026 the board carried 7,987 openings and recorded 131,000 applications from 22,800 candidates — an average of 26 applications per opening, and 132 per opening in front-end development. The first quarter of 2026 carried 22,900 openings, 23% more than the same quarter of 2025. These are one board's own counts for one country, not a market-wide measure, and the average conceals the spread: the ratio differs by a factor of five between specialisations on the same board in the same month.

- Конкуренція серед розробників росте. ІТ-ринок праці у І кварталі 2026. DOU, 2026.
- https://dou.ua/lenta/articles/it-job-market-1-quarter-2026/

### evidence.behind_the_privilege_shield_safeguarding_ai_bias_testing_data_in_employment_decisions_norton_rose_fulbright_2026 — Behind the privilege shield: Safeguarding AI bias-testing data in employment decisions (Norton Rose Fulbright, 2026)

Legal analysis of a May 28, 2026 discovery order in Mobley v. Workday (N.D. Cal.), the pending federal case alleging that Workday's applicant screening tool produces disparate impact against candidates by age, race and disability. The order held that AI bias-testing analyses can be shielded by attorney-client privilege where outside counsel meaningfully directed the testing for legal-advice purposes — quoting the court's finding that "Workday has shown more than mere direction by its attorneys" — while the underlying raw factual data and any regulator-facing reports remain discoverable. Note: this record covers only the privilege ruling; Mobley v. Workday's substantive disparate-impact and "agent of the employer" theories remain contested litigation, not adjudicated fact — an earlier July 2024 order only denied a motion to dismiss those theories on plausibility grounds, and a nationwide ADEA collective was preliminarily certified in May 2025.

- Norton Rose Fulbright, Inside Tech Law (2026, June). Behind the privilege shield: Safeguarding AI bias-testing data in employment decisions.
- https://www.insidetechlaw.com/blog/2026/06/behind-the-privilege-shield-safeguarding-ai-bias-testing-data-in-employment-decisions

### evidence.candidate_dossier_retention_and_talent_pool_transparency_gdpr_art_5_1_e_edpb_guidelines_3_2019 — Candidate Dossier Retention and Talent Pool Transparency (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) & EDPB Guidelines 3/2019)

Article 5(1)(e) of the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) and European Data Protection Board Guidelines 3/2019 establish strict storage limitation principles for recruitment candidate data: holding candidate evaluation records in 'talent pool' pools beyond the initial hiring process requires explicit consent or legitimate interest bounded by stated expiration dates and transparent re-entry criteria.

- Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 5(1)(e) ('kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed').
- https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

### evidence.citizenship_status_as_a_hiring_ground_is_unlawful_unless_a_rule_requires_it — Citizenship status as a hiring ground is unlawful unless a rule requires it (8 U.S.C. § 1324b)

US law makes it "an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual … with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment" because of national origin or, for a protected individual, citizenship status. The exception at § 1324b(a)(2) is the operative part here: citizenship-based discrimination is permitted only where it is "required in order to comply with law, regulation, or executive order, or required by Federal, State, or local government contract". So a rejection that names the right to be employed somewhere is either a requirement someone can point to, or it is unlawful — and the statute obliges the employer to be able to tell the two apart. It reaches recruitment and referral, not only the hiring decision itself. It says nothing about where a candidate lives or which hours they can cover: those are not protected grounds, and a rejection naming them is outside this statute entirely. It binds US employers of more than three people, and it establishes what is permitted, never that any particular rejection occurred.

- 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1)–(a)(2) (unfair immigration-related employment practices).
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b

### evidence.corrected_validity_estimates_reorder_the_selection_methods_and_work_samples_fall_furthest — Corrected validity estimates reorder the selection methods, and work samples fall furthest

Sackett et al. (2022) showed that the range-restriction corrections long used in personnel-selection meta-analyses systematically overstated validity, and re-estimated it. This paper reproduces the full table. Against the prior figures, the corrected operational validities are: structured interviews .42 (was .51), job knowledge tests .40 (was .48), empirically keyed biodata .38 (was .35), work sample tests .33 (was .54), general mental ability .31 (was .51), unstructured interviews .19 (was .38). Two readings matter here. Structured interviews become the strongest single predictor, ahead of general mental ability. And work sample tests fall furthest of anything in the table — .21 — so the familiar claim that a sample of the work is the best available signal no longer holds, though .33 still places it above general mental ability. These are correlations with job performance once hired. Nothing here measures whether a scoring scheme is applied consistently, published in advance, or opened at all.

- Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2023). Revisiting the design of selection systems in light of new findings regarding the validity of widely used predictors. Industrial and Organizational Psychology, 16(3). Reproducing the corrected estimates of Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022), Journal of Applied Psychology 107(11), 2040–2068.
- https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/A20984B138319E3D432E643978BF026D/S175494262300024Xa.pdf/revisiting_the_design_of_selection_systems_in_light_of_new_findings_regarding_the_validity_of_widely_used_predictors.pdf

### evidence.duration_dependence_and_labor_market_conditions_evidence_from_a_field_experiment — Duration Dependence and Labor Market Conditions: Evidence from a Field Experiment

Field experiment sending roughly 12,000 fictitious résumés to about 3,000 postings in 100 US cities: the probability of an interview callback falls sharply with the length of the current unemployment spell (most of the decline within the first eight months) and the penalty is stronger in tighter labor markets — employers use gap length as a screening signal.

- Kroft, K., Lange, F., & Notowidigdo, M. J. (2013). The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(3), 1123–1167.
- https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjt015

### evidence.ecb_deposit_facility_rate_fred — ECB deposit facility rate (FRED)

The ECB deposit facility rate was cut to 0.00% on 11 July 2012, turned negative at −0.10% on 11 June 2014, reached −0.50% on 18 September 2019 and returned to 0.00% on 27 July 2022. Every one of the 3,668 daily observations between 11 July 2012 and 26 July 2022 is at or below zero.

- European Central Bank, ECB Deposit Facility Rate for Euro Area [ECBDFR], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ECBDFR

### evidence.employment_interview_reliability_new_meta_analytic_estimates_by_structure_and_format — Employment Interview Reliability: New Meta-Analytic Estimates by Structure and Format

Meta-analysis of 125 inter-rater reliability coefficients (N = 32,428): reliability is substantially higher for panel interviews than for separate interviews by different interviewers (.74 vs .44) and rises with interview structure — quantifying how much interviewer variance, rather than candidate performance, drives divergent verdicts.

- Huffcutt, A. I., Culbertson, S. S., & Weyhrauch, W. S. (2013). International Journal of Selection and Assessment, 21(3), 264–276.
- https://doi.org/10.1111/ijsa.12036

### evidence.employment_of_young_software_developers_stanford_digital_economy_lab — Employment of young software developers (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)

In payroll records covering 3.5–5 million workers a month, employment of software developers aged 22–25 fell by close to 20% between its late-2022 peak and September 2025, while employment for older workers in the same occupation did not fall. This is the paper's raw descriptive series for one occupation; its headline regression result — a 16% relative decline for ages 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations, controlling for firm-level shocks — is a different figure and should not be conflated with it.

- Brynjolfsson, E., Chandar, B., & Chen, R. (2025). Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence. Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 13 November 2025.
- https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2025/11/CanariesintheCoalMine_Nov25.pdf

### evidence.federal_funds_target_range_and_effective_rate_fred — Federal funds target range and effective rate (FRED)

The FOMC held the federal funds target range at 0.00–0.25% from 16 December 2008 to 15 December 2015 and again from 16 March 2020 to 16 March 2022. In every full month inside those two windows the effective federal funds rate stayed between 0.05% and 0.22%. Verified against the full daily DFEDTARU/DFEDTARL series (2,556 and 731 daily observations respectively, no other value in either window) and the monthly FEDFUNDS series.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Federal Funds Target Range — Upper Limit [DFEDTARU], Lower Limit [DFEDTARL] and Federal Funds Effective Rate [FEDFUNDS], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU

### evidence.fomc_policy_rate_decisions_open_market_operations — FOMC policy rate decisions (Open Market Operations)

The FOMC raised the federal funds target range to 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023, the peak of the tightening cycle, and held it there until the 25 basis point reduction of 18 September 2024 — roughly fourteen months.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Open Market Operations, policy tools archive.
- https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm

### evidence.hidden_workers_untapped_talent_hbs_accenture — Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent (HBS / Accenture)

Survey of 8,000 workers and 2,250 executives in the US, UK and Germany on automated hiring. 88% of employers agree that qualified high-skill candidates are vetted out of the process by applicant tracking systems because they do not match the exact criteria of the job description; the report attributes a large "hidden worker" population to configurable ATS exclusion rules and knock-out filters.

- Fuller, J. B., Raman, M., Sage-Gavin, E., & Hines, K. (2021). Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent. Harvard Business School Project on Managing the Future of Work & Accenture.
- https://www.hbs.edu/managing-the-future-of-work/research/hidden-workers-untapped-talent

### evidence.hires_information_sector_bls_jolts — Hires, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025, a decline of 367,000 or 28.9%. The measure counts hiring flows, not layoff announcements.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTU510000000000000HIL (Hires, information, total US, not seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTU510000000000000HIL

### evidence.hires_rate_total_private_bls_jolts — Hires rate, total private (BLS JOLTS)

The seasonally adjusted hires rate for total private employment was 3.7% in June 2026 (preliminary), a full percentage point below its June 2022 level of 4.7%: fewer positions per hundred jobs are being filled each month.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS100000000000000HIR (Hires rate, total private, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS100000000000000HIR

### evidence.internal_candidacy_and_public_competition_governance_5_u_s_c_2301_uk_civil_service_management_code — Internal Candidacy and Public Competition Governance (5 U.S.C. § 2301 & UK Civil Service Management Code)

5 U.S.C. § 2301 states merit-system principles for the US federal civil service, including recruitment from appropriate sources and selection after fair and open competition. UK Civil Service recruitment rules likewise govern appointment on merit after fair and open competition, subject to defined exceptions. These are public-service rules; they do not create a general private-sector duty to disclose an internal candidate or prove that an external process is deceptive.

- 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(1) ('Recruitment should be from qualified individuals from appropriate sources in an endeavor to achieve a work force from all segments of society, and selection and advancement should be determined solely on the basis of relative ability, knowledge, and skills, after fair and open competition which assures that all receive equal opportunity.').
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/5/2301

### evidence.job_openings_information_sector_bls_jolts — Job openings, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Job openings in the US information sector averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 a month in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026, against an April 2022 peak of 274,000.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS510000000000000JOL (Job openings, information, total US, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS510000000000000JOL

### evidence.job_seekers_beware_of_ghost_jobs_clarify_capital_survey_of_hiring_managers — Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs (Clarify Capital survey of hiring managers)

Survey of 1,045 managers involved in hiring (fielded 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022) on job postings kept live without active hiring: about half keep postings open because they are "always open to new people", 43% cite giving the impression that the company is growing or keeping existing employees motivated, one in three postings had been active for more than 30 days, and one in four respondents did not plan to fill the role for three months or longer.

- Clarify Capital (2022). Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs. Survey of 1,045 hiring managers, 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022.
- https://clarifycapital.com/job-seekers-beware-of-ghost-jobs-survey

### evidence.kpmg_venture_pulse_q4_2021 — KPMG Venture Pulse, Q4 2021

Global venture capital investment totalled $671 billion across 2021, the highest annual figure in the series, of which $171.4 billion was invested in Q4 2021 across 8,710 deals. Underlying data provided by PitchBook as of 31 December 2021.

- KPMG Private Enterprise, Venture Pulse Q4 2021: Global analysis of venture funding, 19 January 2022, p. 7.
- https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmg/xx/pdf/2022/01/venture-pulse-q4-2021.pdf

### evidence.layoffs_and_discharges_information_sector_bls_jolts — Layoffs and discharges, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Official separations in the US information sector were 451,000 in 2022, 399,000 in 2023, 395,000 in 2024 and 447,000 in 2025 — roughly flat across the period, and without the year-to-year collapse reported by tracked-layoff counts over the same span.
